To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

family history of brain tumors is not associated with increased risk of childhood brain tumor; family history of birth defect in maternal relatives is associated with a moderate elevation in risk of childhood tumor; family history is associated with increased risk in a dose-response fashion for brain tumors of histologic type other than medulloblastomas and astrocytomas; and family history is associated in a dose-response manner with risk of brain tumors that arise in the infratentorial portion of the brain.
maternal history of birth defects, particularly among female relatives, was modestly associated with risk of brain tumors, but that family history of tumors was not associated with risk.
maternal family history of a birth defect is associated with a 2-fold increase in risk of a brain tumor in a child.

the role of family and social factors in the development of childhood brain tumors.

the role of family factors and other risk factors in childhood brain tumors, and we have found that family history of birth defect in mothers and maternal female relatives may be associated with an increase in risk of brain tumor.
the etiologic factors associated with the occurrence of brain tumors in young children and the role of genetic factors in the etiology of these tumors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of family histories in risk of brain tumors is not well established and that the data are insufficient to support the hypothesis of a genetic component to the etiology of brain tumors.

the family history of childhood brain tumor is of limited importance as a risk factor for the development of childhood brain tumors, although the family history of birth defect may be of some importance.
the risk of childhood brain tumor is increased by a history of birth defect in the mother or maternal relatives, but is otherwise not increased by a family history of tumors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
family history of birth defect in maternal relatives was associated with childhood brain tumor.
there is an association between maternal family history of congenital anomalies and risk of childhood brain tumor.
family history of birth defect in the maternal line appears to be associated with increased risk of childhood brain tumor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of childhood brain tumor does not increase with the family history of cancer, but does increase with family history of birth defect.

the risk of brain tumors is increased in children with a maternal history of birth defects, and this risk is particularly high for infratentorial brain tumors and brain tumors of other histologic types.
there is no evidence that family history of cancer or other tumors is associated with risk of childhood brain tumor.
